newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus election boss wants referendums delayed.
newsitem.headline: Belarus election boss wants referendums delayed.

text.p: The head of the Belarussian Central Electoral Commission said on Wednesday that his group would not recognise either of two planned constitutional referendums, one proposed by the president and the other by parliament.
Nikolai Gonchar said his commission did not have time to draw up lists of voters and to set up local electoral bodies.
"Holding a referendum (on November 7) is impossible from a technical point of view," he told a news conference. "Holding a referendum is not possible even as late as November 24."

President Alexander Lukashenko, a hardline advocate of union with Russia, has called a referendum on the November 7 anniversary of the Bolshevik revolution on a new constitution that he says will enable him to rule for 10 more years.
Parliament, whose factions last month united to oppose Lukashenko, has called its own vote for November 24 on a different constitution which abolishes the post of president.
Gonchar said even the later date was not feasible.
"We cannot guarantee the observation of all democratic procedures and are asking (both sides) to hold the referendums later," said Gonchar.
Minsk streets are flush with posters urging voters to take part in the plebiscite, but only one poster near the KGB security service urges citizens to vote on November 7.
Lukashenko has called an "All-Belarussian meeting" on October 19 to seek backing for his referendum, but opposition members say it will be attended only by loyal apparatchiks.
Lukashenko's aides said the president would find $2 million of non-budget funds to organise the refendum.
Earlier this week 111 of 199 parliamentary deputies signed an appeal to Lukashenko to find a compromise.
They said they would agree with Lukashenko's proposal of a two-chamber parliament but that the upper house should be a mainly elected body instead of a presidentially-appointed one.

Lukashenko, elected Belarus's first post-Soviet president in 1994, has since suspended trade unions, shut down newspapers and put the brakes on market reforms. Some 200 people were jailed for demonstrating against a community pact with Moscow.
Deputy Prime Minister Sergei Ling said on Tuesday that Belarus would amend its new economic plan after criticism from the World Bank and International Monetary Fund.

"We are being criticised for government interference in the level of the rouble and prices, slow privatisation and strong government regulations," Ling told a news conference. "We will make changes, but with Belarus's interests in mind."
Both president and parliamentarians have been looking for support from the Kremlin and Russian President Boris Yeltsin recently urged Lukashenko to find a compromise.
But security chief Alexander Lebed and Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov, both possible contenders in any new presidential race to succeed Yeltsin, have praised the Belarussian president.
